newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Never mind the crash, Philippine economy seems OK.
newsitem.headline: Never mind the crash, Philippine economy seems OK.

text.p: Philippine shares may be diving to new lows, but the country's economy looks fine and should eventually lure back investors, economists said on Wednesday.
"People are liable to bolt at the moment without thinking very much," a Singapore-based economist said of the savage selling that has hit the Philippine market in the past two days.
Fears of a repeat in the Philippines of Thailand's property crash have been blamed for much of the selling, which has pushed Manila's share index 20 percent below its record high in February.
"I don't see any fundamental economic reason for this...I think the market has over-reacted," Roman Azanza, director of Crosby UBP Securities, said.
While the share market had been getting pricey, and was certainly due for a big correction, the outlook was still positive, he said.

Economists said the level of bank loans to the property sector was not high, especially compared to some other countries in the region, though a glut in certain areas of the booming real estate market was probably inevitable.
The experience of the Philippines was not the same as in Thailand, they said.
"Real estate here has not been financed by foreign loans (like Thailand)," said Teresa Paningco, economist at the University of Asia and the Pacific.
She said several areas of the property market, such as housing, still showed strong demand while occupancy levels were about the highest in the region.

"But the Central Bank cap on property loans (announced on Tuesday) for me validates the fact that there must be some truth to the concerns, but not enough to cause this collapse," managing director of Angping and Associates Securities, Wilfred Son Keng Po, said.

"The market is equating consolidation with a demise. The Philippine economy is entering a consolidation phase...generally it is doing OK, though maybe the signals are not as strong as anticipated," he added.
The early signs are that Philippine economic growth has been moving up steadily since the start of the year, according to officials.

Socorro Zingapan, a senior official at the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), said although it was too early to predict the first quarter GNP growth rate, there had been good export growth in the first two months.
The government is predicting gross national product growth this year of up to eight percent. Economists say that even if growth is a bit lower, it will still feed into corporate profits.
Growth last year of 6.8 percent was the highest in six years.

Economists expressed little concern about the impact of the share market fall on monetary policy, even though the Central Bank was forced to push up interest rates on Wednesday to protect the peso, in what it called a pre-emptive move.
"If anything they have been over-prudent on monetary policy. The Central Bank has been trying to protect the peso to keep inflation low," Paningco said.
